title: Indian-Origin Couple Sentenced in UK Over Fake Covid PPE Deals
excerpt: Jogesh Bhandari was jailed for eight years and his wife given a suspended sentence after a five-week trial over nitrile-glove contracts that were paid for and never delivered.
body:
• Jogesh Bhandari, 59, of Loughborough, was sentenced to eight years in prison on October 16 for fraud and money laundering over fake Covid PPE supply deals, the National Crime Agency said.
  • His wife Meenakshi Bhandari received a two-year sentence suspended for two years plus 250 hours of unpaid work on October 7; associate Craig Morris, 43, was jailed for three years and nine months.
  • The group took payments for millions of boxes of nitrile gloves — including $2.7 million in December 2020 and over $3.18 million in early 2021 — that were never delivered, investigators found.
  • Money was spent on a Porsche, other luxury cars, watches, jewellery and home renovations while hospitals waited for supplies.

An Indian-origin businessman has been jailed for eight years in Britain for defrauding companies through fake personal protective equipment deals during the Covid-19 pandemic and spending the proceeds on luxury cars, watches and home renovations. Jogesh Bhandari, 59, from Loughborough, was sentenced on October 16 after failing to attend two earlier hearings citing health issues, prompting a judge to order his arrest, according to Britain's National Crime Agency (NCA), in reporting carried by PTI.

The scheme

Bhandari and Craig Morris, 43, set up a company in 2020 — named in court as Banton — to trade nitrile gloves, then in extreme demand. They worked with Frank Labruzzo, a US assistant attorney general at the Louisiana State Department of Justice, who provided a fraudulent escrow service, investigators found. In November 2020 Bhandari agreed to supply 12 million boxes of gloves; money paid into the escrow account was instead transferred to him, Labruzzo and other companies. The following month he received another $2.7 million and withdrew $500,000 almost immediately to settle debts. In early 2021 he was paid more than $3.18 million for gloves intended for US hospitals that never arrived, and a final deal brought $1.35 million for the first two planned shipments, according to the court reporting summarised by Opera News.

Sentences for all three

The three were convicted of fraud and money laundering after a five-week trial in July. Meenakshi (Meena) Bhandari, a former pharmacist, was found guilty of money laundering and sentenced on October 7 to a two-year prison term suspended for two years, with 250 hours of unpaid community work. Morris was jailed for three years and nine months at the same hearing. Sentencing Jogesh Bhandari, Judge William Harbage KC called him the "driving force" and "directing mind" of the company used for the fraudulent deals, and said remorse expressed in a letter was "difficult to accept given how vigorously you contested these charges."

"While Bhandari was picking up his brand new luxury car and talking about how he couldn't stop smiling, healthcare facilities had not received the vital PPE they needed at a time when demand was exponential."

— Paul Boniface, National Crime Agency

Investigators said the group spent hundreds of thousands of pounds on house renovations and luxury cars, including £126,000 on a Porsche, plus an Audi A5, a Land Rover Discovery, jewellery and holiday packages. "These defendants took an opportunity to target legitimate businesses and line their own pockets for a lavish lifestyle during a pandemic that caused uncertainty around the world," said Paul Boniface, an NCA operations manager. The agency said it will continue to target fraudsters who cause significant harm to the UK economy. The case closes one of the pandemic era's PPE prosecutions — contracts written in the emergency of 2020, unwound in court six years later.
